list.expr: {job="integrations/kubernetes/eventhandler", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespacepattern", type="Normal", kind="Pod", name=~"$pod"} | logfmt | reason="Killing" | line_format "Killing {{.name}} — {{.msg}}"

list.expr: {job="integrations/kubernetes/eventhandler", cluster=~"$cluster", namespace=~"$namespacepattern", kind=~"Deployment|StatefulSet", name=~"($pod_controller).*"} | logfmt | line_format "{{.kind}} {{.name}}: {{.reason}} — {{.msg}}"

list.name: OOMKilled

panels.description: Connected clients (`arb_feed_clients_current`) and, on the rust relay only, the caught-up subset being served new messages live (`arb_feed_clients_live`). A large current-minus-live gap means many clients are still draining backlog. Go relays export no `_live` series, so that series is absent on a nitro-node row.
panels.title: Connections

panels.description: Client connections rejected for exceeding the per-IP connection limit. The Go relay (nitro-node) exports `arb_feed_clients_limited`; the rust relay (arb-relay, v0.5+) exports `arb_feed_clients_limit_rejected` for `--ip-connections-limit`. Only one series exists per relay job, so a flat line on one of them is expected — but *both* empty means the relay is older than v0.5 or the limiter is inert, not that nothing is being rejected. Check **IP Limit Enforcement** before reading this as zero.
panels.title: Connection Limit Rate

panels.description: Why the rust relay's `--ip-connections-limit` did or did not apply to a connection. **unknown ip** — the `--client-ip-header` was missing, so the limit was *not enforced*; a configured limiter that is inert shows up here. **malformed ip header** — the header could not be parsed, so the limit was enforced against the TCP peer address (typically the proxy, i.e. shared across clients). **exempt ip** — client IP is private or loopback. Sustained unknown/malformed rates mean the rejection count in **Connection Limit Rate** understates reality. Empty on Go relays and on rust relays before v0.5.

targets.legendFormat: malformed ip header (fell back to peer) - {{cluster}}

panels.title: IP Limit Enforcement (rust relay)

panels.description:
Clients the relay disconnected for falling behind the broadcast (`arb_feed_clients_lagged`) — the client's send queue overflowed and it was evicted rather than allowed to stall the broadcaster. This is a *subset of disconnects*, which is why it also appears as a third series on **Connect/Disconnect Rate**; here it is broken out per pod.

One pod shedding laggards while its peers stay flat is local to that box — its egress, CPU or network path. Every pod shedding at once is not a relay fault: either demand the fleet cannot feed, or an upstream stall pushing a burst of backlogged messages through every broadcaster at once. Cross-read the fleet-wide case with **Block Rate** and **Total Transmit Rate**.

Distinct from **Connection Limit Rate**, which refuses a connection up front; a lag drop kills one already being served.

Empty — *not zero* — on Go relays and on rust relays before v0.7.2, which export no such counter. A pod missing from this panel is unknown, not idle: check its image tag in **Version** on the same row before reading a gap as no drops.
panels.title: Clients Dropped for Lag (rust relay)

panels.description: Pod egress divided by connected clients — the average bandwidth one feed subscriber costs. Useful for capacity work (egress per additional client) and for spotting a feed whose per-client cost has jumped. Two caveats: the numerator is *total* pod egress from cAdvisor, so it also carries metric scrapes, health checks and upstream chatter — a fixed overhead that is negligible at thousands of clients but dominates at a handful (an idle relay with no clients attached still transmits on the order of 10 KB/s). And at zero connected clients the ratio is undefined, so the line breaks rather than spiking.

targets.expr: sum(rate(container_network_transmit_bytes_total{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern"}[$__rate_interval]) and on (pod) arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) by (cluster) / (sum(arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) by (cluster) > 0)

panels.title: Bandwidth per Connection

panels.description:
Relay CPU divided by connected clients, per pod — the average CPU one feed subscriber costs, in millicores. Useful for capacity work (CPU per additional client) and as the compression lever: a pod whose clients negotiated `permessage-deflate` spends a fraction of the CPU per client that a pod serving uncompressed clients does, so a pair of otherwise identical pods is the measurement. Pods on different hardware are not like for like — client mix, message rate and CPU clock all differ; **Clock-Normalised CPU per Connection** removes the clock part of that.

Three caveats. The numerator is the container's cgroup, so kernel work outside it — softirq, where much of the fan-out cost lands — is only partly charged here; a pod can read as cheap while the host itself is short of CPU, so check host CPU before concluding otherwise. Fixed per-pod cost (upstream feed handling, backlog trimming, scrapes) is divided by whatever is attached, so at a handful of clients this reads as base cost per client, not the marginal cost of one more. And a pod absorbing a reconnect storm pays backlog sends here, so a spike can be churn rather than steady-state cost — cross-read **Connect/Disconnect Rate**.

targets.expr: 1000 * sum(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern",image!=""}[$__rate_interval]) and on (pod, cluster) arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) by (pod, cluster) / (sum(arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) by (pod, cluster) > 0)

panels.title: CPU per Connection (mCPU)

panels.description:
**CPU per Connection** multiplied by the host's rated CPU clock — per-client cost as cycles per second, so pods on hardware of different clock speeds can be compared. Where relays run on more than one class of host, raw millicores understate the per-client work done by whichever host has the slower clock.

The multiplier is `node_cpu_scaling_frequency_max_hertz`, a static hardware property, *not* the live scaling frequency: cores clock down when a host is idle, so normalising by the instantaneous value would divide out part of the saving being measured — a pod that got cheaper would report a lower clock and be credited for it twice.

This removes the clock confound, not the architecture one. Cycles are not equal work across microarchitectures, and turbo residency and SMT differ, so read a cross-hardware gap as indicative and keep the measurement to pods on matching hosts. The clock is matched to a pod by host: the address part of `instance`, without the port, on its cAdvisor series and on node_exporter. Under kube-prometheus-stack both carry the node's IP. Empty — *not zero* — wherever node_exporter reports no cpufreq, which is usual on virtualised instances, or where the two scrapes name the host differently; use **CPU per Connection (mCPU)** there.

targets.expr: (sum by (cluster, pod, host) (label_replace(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern",image!=""}[$__rate_interval]), "host", "$1", "instance", "([^:]+).*") and on (pod, cluster) arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) / on (cluster, pod) group_left() (sum by (cluster, pod) (arb_feed_clients_current{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}) > 0)) * on (cluster, host) group_left() avg by (cluster, host) (label_replace(node_cpu_scaling_frequency_max_hertz{cluster=~"$cluster"}, "host", "$1", "instance", "([^:]+).*"))

panels.title: Clock-Normalised CPU per Connection

panels.description: Client connections admitted per second, split by whether they asked for `permessage-deflate` (`arb_feed_clients_compression_negotiated` / `arb_feed_clients_compression_not_requested`). **negotiated** is uptake, not delivery: a client that negotiates and then fails to inflate still counts. **not requested** is counted whatever the `--compression` setting is, so while it keeps climbing some client is not asking. Under `--compression=off` negotiated is pinned at zero and every connection lands in not requested. Empty on Go relays and on rust relays before v0.7.
panels.title: Compression Negotiation (rust relay)

panels.description: Share of connections admitted since pod start that negotiated compression. Read the inverse as the pre-flight for `--compression=required`: at 97% uptake, `required` would refuse the remaining 3%. Before flipping it, identify who they are — a chained arb-relay never offers compression on its own upstream connection, so it sits in the refused population. Counters are cumulative, so this resets when a pod restarts. Empty on Go relays and on rust relays before v0.7.
panels.title: Compression Uptake % (rust relay)

panels.description: Go relay (nitro-node) client connections dropped because its worker pool was exhausted (`arb_feed_clients_failed_worker`). The rust relay has no worker pool and exports no equivalent, so this panel is empty — *not zero* — on any rust relay job. Check the image tag in **Version** on the same row before reading a gap here as no drops.
panels.title: Out of Workers (Go relay only)

panels.description: Messages served from the relay's backlog cache to each admitted client (`arb_feed_clients_cache_sent` histogram), as p50/p90/p99 and the mean over the rate interval. This is how far behind clients are when they connect, and the socket work that the REST feed backlog takes over as clients adopt it: with **Backfill-capable Connections** climbing, the upper quantiles here should fall, because a capable client gets at most one published chunk plus the unsettled tail over the socket and fetches the rest over REST. A reconnect storm after an outage shows as a spike in the upper quantiles. Empty — *not zero* — on Go relays.
panels.title: Backlog Messages per Connection (rust relay)

panels.description: How far behind the live tip a client's requested resume point was when it connected (`arb_feed_clients_requested_gap_depth` histogram), as p50/p90/p99 over the rate interval. Read it against the socket catch-up window, `(--max-catchup-chunks + 1) * --chunk-size + --chunk-settle-messages` (105 messages at the defaults): a gap inside that window is served entirely over the socket whether or not the client is backfill-capable, so the REST backlog changes nothing for it. Only deeper gaps move to REST, which is why this panel decides how much of **Backlog Messages per Connection** the archive can take over. Empty — *not zero* — on Go relays and on older rust relays.
panels.title: Requested Gap Depth (rust relay)

panels.description: Admitted connections per second from clients that advertised REST backfill with the `Arbitrum-Feed-Backfill` header (`arb_feed_clients_backfill_capable`), against all admitted connections (`arb_feed_clients_connect`). This is the adoption curve of the REST feed backlog. A capable client is served at most one published chunk plus the unsettled tail over the socket and fetches anything older from the REST archive — whether or not this relay runs `--rest-enable`. So a non-zero capable rate on a fleet with no reachable archive means those clients are being capped with nothing to fill the gap from; check the **Feed REST Archive** row of the archive job before enabling the client anywhere. Empty — *not zero* — on Go relays and on rust relays before v0.7.5.
panels.title: Backfill-capable Connections (rust relay)

panels.description: HTTP→WebSocket upgrade failures, split into disjoint parts that stack to the `arb_feed_clients_failed_upgrade` total. **rate limited** is the per-IP limit rejections (`arb_feed_clients_limit_rejected`, rust v0.5+), which are a *subset* of failed upgrades — so it is broken out here rather than counted twice alongside **other** (TLS/mTLS handshake and protocol errors). On relays with no rejection counter the whole total shows as **other**.

targets.expr: sum(irate(arb_feed_clients_failed_upgrade{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}[$__rate_interval])) by (cluster) - (sum(irate(arb_feed_clients_limit_rejected{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}[$__rate_interval])) by (cluster) or sum(irate(arb_feed_clients_failed_upgrade{cluster=~"$cluster",namespace=~"$namespacepattern", job="$relayjob"}[$__rate_interval])) by (cluster) * 0)

panels.title: Failed WS Upgrade

panels.description: Upstream feed divergence as seen by the rust relay — the fastest way to clear or implicate the relay during a feed incident. **reorgs** are confirmed (changed `blockHash`) replacements; **possible reorgs** are replacements of undetermined severity; **below-confirmed reorgs** changed a blockHash for an already-confirmed, trimmed sequence number and *cannot be rebroadcast* (counts messages, so a replaying upstream re-counts each pass); **flaps** are benign feed flaps. Any non-zero reorg rate here means the divergence originates upstream of the relay. Empty on Go relays.
panels.title: Feed Reorgs & Flaps (rust relay)

panels.description: Buffered sequence numbers whose payload diverges from what was already broadcast live — un-adopted possible reorgs (`arb_feed_diverged_seqs_current`). This is a gauge, not a rate: a value that stays above zero means the relay's backlog and its live broadcast disagree, so clients replaying from cache can receive different bytes than clients that were live. Empty on Go relays.
panels.title: Diverged Sequence Numbers (rust relay)

panels.description: **old messages dropped** — below-window messages too old to classify or rebroadcast (`arb_feed_old_messages_dropped_total`); a sustained rate means an upstream is replaying far behind the relay's window. **duplicates** — byte-identical messages received again while still buffered and deduped, never rebroadcast (`arb_feed_duplicates_total`); benign on its own, but a jump usually accompanies an upstream reconnect. Empty on Go relays.
panels.title: Dropped & Deduped Messages (rust relay)

panels.description: Chunks published per second (`arb_feed_chunks_published_total`), per pod. A chunk is published once it holds `--chunk-size` messages and the feed has moved `--chunk-settle-messages` past its end, so at a steady message rate this is a flat line of one chunk per `--chunk-size` messages. A pause while **Block Rate** keeps moving means the archive is not publishing. After a restart or a feed gap the first partial chunk is never published, which shows as a short pause here and a step in **messages skipped** on **Chunk Trims**.
panels.title: Chunk Publish Rate (REST archive)

panels.description: Published chunks this archive still serves (`arb_feed_chunks_published_current`), per pod. A chunk is dropped once every message in it is finalized on the parent chain, or oldest-first while the archive is over `--rest-max-archive-bytes`, so this is the window a backfilling node can fetch over REST: roughly the unconfirmed tail of the feed, in chunks. It is held in memory only, so a restart empties it and the line climbs back from zero. Replicas build their own copies independently, so their lines track each other without matching exactly.
panels.title: Chunks Retained (REST archive)

panels.description: Gzipped bytes of the retained chunks (`arb_feed_chunks_bytes_current`), per pod. Bounded by `--rest-max-archive-bytes`; one chunk is always kept even if it alone exceeds the cap. This is the chunk bodies only, not the process. If **Chunk Trims** shows **byte cap** trims while this sits at the cap, the archive is dropping history that nodes may still want: raise the cap.
panels.title: Archive Size (REST archive)

panels.description: Why chunks and messages leave the archive, per second. **finalized** is the normal lifecycle: every message in the chunk is confirmed on the parent chain. **byte cap** trims happen before finalization and mean the archive is too small for its retention window. **reorg below frontier** is a feed reorg underneath an already-published chunk and needs looking at. **messages skipped** are messages not archived while waiting for the next chunk boundary, which jumps after a restart or a feed gap and is flat otherwise. **messages dropped at gap** are messages discarded from the chunk being built because of a forward feed gap. The last four should sit at zero in steady state. Chunk series are on the left axis and message series on the right, so a jump in messages skipped after a restart does not flatten the chunk lines.
panels.title: Chunk Trims (REST archive)

panels.description: What the archive answered, per second, stacked. **info** is `/feed/v1/info`. **chunk served** is a published chunk body, so it tracks backfill load. **not settled** is a 404 for a chunk the feed has not moved past yet, which is clients polling at the tip and is low in steady state. **evicted** is a chunk the archive no longer holds; a spike means clients want older history than it keeps. **not found** is a path outside the API. **bad request** is a start that is not a multiple of `--chunk-size`, or a query string. **not acceptable** is a client that did not offer gzip. **internal error** is a server failure. The last three should be zero. With a cache or CDN in front of the archive, only requests that reached the origin count here; a flat **chunk served** under real client load is the cache doing its job, not an idle archive.
panels.title: REST Requests by Outcome (REST archive)
